reference.source: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology / Endocrine Society clinical guidance
clinicalPearls: An autosomal recessive defect of the enzyme that converts androgens to oestrogens, so both fetus and mother lose the placental oestrogen buffer
A 46,XX fetus is virilised at birth (ambiguous genitalia) because placental androgens are not aromatised to oestrogens
The mother often becomes virilised during pregnancy, with acne, hirsutism and voice change that resolve after delivery
In affected females puberty fails to progress, with primary amenorrhoea, undetectable oestrogen, high gonadotropins and polycystic ovaries
Both sexes show tall stature, delayed bone age initially but unfused growth plates, and eventual osteoporosis because oestrogen is essential for epiphyseal closure and bone mineralisation
Metabolic consequences include insulin resistance and abnormal lipids, reflecting oestrogen's systemic roles
Management centres on oestrogen replacement to induce puberty, close epiphyses and protect bone, tailored to sex and age
reference.pathophysiology: Aromatase, encoded by CYP19A1, converts androgenic precursors into oestrogens in the placenta, gonads, adipose tissue, bone and brain. Biallelic loss-of-function variants abolish this conversion, so androgens accumulate and oestrogens are deficient. During pregnancy the placenta cannot aromatise fetal and maternal androgens, virilising a 46,XX fetus and transiently the mother. After birth the persistent oestrogen deficiency prevents normal pubertal development in girls, drives hypergonadotropic ovarian stimulation with cyst formation, and removes the oestrogen signal required for growth-plate fusion and bone mineral accrual, producing tall stature with delayed skeletal maturation followed by osteoporosis. Insulin resistance and dyslipidaemia reflect the loss of oestrogen action in metabolic tissues.
additionalDifferentials: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (21-hydroxylase deficiency) causing virilisation of a 46,XX infant
Maternal virilising tumour or luteoma of pregnancy
Complete androgen insensitivity syndrome (in the differential of delayed puberty)
additionalInvestigations: Karyotype to confirm 46,XX in a virilised infant
Serum oestradiol (low or undetectable) with elevated androgens and gonadotropins
Molecular analysis of the CYP19A1 gene
Pelvic ultrasound showing enlarged multicystic ovaries
Bone age radiograph and bone mineral density assessment
Metabolic profile including fasting glucose, insulin and lipids
redFlags: Ambiguous genitalia in a newborn requiring exclusion of salt-wasting congenital adrenal hyperplasia
Maternal virilisation during pregnancy prompting evaluation for the fetal disorder
Progressive tall stature with unfused epiphyses and low bone density
reference.prognosis: With oestrogen replacement, pubertal development, epiphyseal closure and bone health can be restored and metabolic disturbances improved; maternal virilisation resolves after delivery. Untreated disease leads to eunuchoid tall stature, severe osteoporosis and metabolic complications.
pitfalls: Mistaking the virilised 46,XX infant for congenital adrenal hyperplasia and missing the aromatase defect
Overlooking maternal virilisation in pregnancy as a diagnostic clue
Delaying oestrogen replacement and allowing continued linear growth and bone loss
Neglecting metabolic surveillance for insulin resistance and dyslipidaemia
references: Endocrine Society clinical practice guidance on disorders of sex development
